USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current tariff posture and enter the G20 Xi meeting seeking a temporary truce — no new escalation, no concessions. The $300B tariff threat remains our leverage; deploying it now would be costly and premature when talks may resume. Let the existing pressure work while managing domestic fallout through the $16B farm aid package already announced.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderately elevated (threat_score +0.35) but not acute, for the following reasons grounded in PIT evidence:

(a) WHAT DRIVES THE THREAT READING: The trade war's costs are asymmetric but real for the US. Research shows tariff costs fall entirely on US importers and consumers, not Chinese exporters (Econofact/Fajgelbaum et al.; Amiti, Redding, Weinstein). The Fed Bank of New York estimates $831/year per household. Soybean exports to China collapsed from $14B to near-zero, forcing a $16B farm bailout (USDA May 23). The Huawei Entity List (May 16) backfired — US chipmakers (Qualcomm -4%, Micron -3%, Qorvo -7%) lost revenue, and by late June companies like Micron and Intel found legal workarounds (de minimis rule), undermining the policy's coherence (LA Times, June 26). China's rare earth threats (Xi's Jiangxi visit May 20, NDRC/People's Daily warnings May 29-30) expose a genuine US supply chain vulnerability — 80% of mining, 95% of processing controlled by China, with no domestic alternative for 5-10 years. Morgan Stanley's business conditions index posted its worst one-month drop in history (Foreign Policy Journal, June 21). The World Bank cut global growth to 2.6%, IMF warned of $455B in GDP losses.

However, the direct GDP drag is still modest — estimated 0.3pp for existing tariffs (Oxford Economics), and US direct trade exposure to China is lower than the reverse (exports 0.9% vs 3.5% of GDP per QNB analysis). China's economy is suffering more acutely through the direct trade channel, with Huawei slashing supplier orders by 20-30% (Nikkei/Business Insider, June 5). The US retains the $300B tariff threat as leverage, which China has no equivalent counter to.

(b) WHAT JUSTIFIES THE ACTION STANCE: With the Trump-Xi G20 meeting scheduled for June 28-29 (confirmed June 18), this is the wrong moment to escalate or concede. Escalation — specifically imposing the $300B tranche — would hit consumer goods (60% of remaining imports per QNB analysis), raising prices on electronics, clothing, and household items visible to voters. It would also destroy the G20 meeting before it happens. Concession is premature: China has not made structural reform commitments on IP, tech transfer, or enforcement — only purchase commitments were discussed, and even those collapsed in May when China 'renegotiated' (Trump's May 5 tweet). The hold position preserves maximum optionality. If the G20 produces a Buenos Aires-style truce (which experts expect per Guardian/NPR/CSIS), talks resume and pressure continues. If it fails, the $300B tariff remains available. Meanwhile, US companies are already finding ways to work around the Huawei ban, reducing the urgency of that pressure point. The farm aid package ($16B, announced May 23) buys political space in key agricultural states through at least Q3 2019.
key_factors: Tariff costs fully borne by US importers/consumers, not Chinese exporters — $831/household/year
Huawei Entity List backfiring: US chipmakers finding legal workarounds, policy coherence undermined
China rare earth leverage (80% mining, 95% processing) — genuine supply chain vulnerability with 5-10yr fix
Farm crisis severe — soybean exports collapsed, $16B bailout needed, rural political pressure mounting
G20 Xi meeting June 28-29 — wrong moment to escalate or concede, preserve optionality
$300B tariff threat still available as leverage; 60% is consumer goods — deploying now risks voter backlash
China suffering more acutely through direct trade channel — Huawei cutting orders 20-30%, leverage is asymmetric
Morgan Stanley business conditions index worst monthly drop in history — sentiment deterioration

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets that negotiations are going 'too slowly' and that China is attempting to 'renegotiate.' Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
Trump and Xi agree by phone to meet at the G20 in Osaka.

US exports to and imports from China account for 0.9% and 2.7% of GDP, Chinese exports to and imports from the US account for 3.5% and 1.1% of GDP. Tariffs are currently boosting core inflation by around 20 basis points in the US. S&P 500 and Shanghai Composite plummeted by 3.6% and 5.6% since early May 2019.

Recent research shows that the new tariffs are completely passed through into increased prices paid by US importers. The Trade Partnership estimates steel/aluminum + 25% tariff on $250B would cut US employment by 934,000 and cost the average family of four $767 a year.

Trump unveiled a $16 billion bailout for farmers. Federal Reserve Bank of New York said Trump's tariffs will cost the average American household $831 annually. Soybean prices fell from $10.89 to $8.68 per bushel.

Micron Technology started shipping some components to Huawei after lawyers studied export restrictions. Intel also resumed sales. Companies exploiting de minimis rule — if less than 25% of technology originates in the US, it may not be covered by the ban.

NDRC statement: 'If anyone wants to use the products made from our rare earth exports to try to counter China's development, then the people from the southern Jiangxi Communist revolutionary base would not be happy.' People's Daily: 'We remind the US not to underestimate China's ability to defend its rights to development.'
Huawei slashed orders to supply chain by as much as 30%. Lowered predictions for smartphone shipments in H2 2019 by 20-30% after the ban. TSMC confirmed Huawei scaled back orders.

Morgan Stanley's business conditions index just took the worst one-month hit in its history. IMF warned trade wars could wipe $455 billion off global GDP in 2020. World Bank estimated world economy would only expand by 2.6%.
